notes.meaning: Paul asks a question that his readers would naturally wonder about after hearing that God judges everyone by the heart. If outward religion does not automatically save someone, a person might ask what special benefit Jewish people had. This question introduces an objection to show why God's special covenant with Israel still mattered.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars understand the oracles of God to mean specifically God's covenant promises or predictions of the Messiah, rather than the entire Old Testament.

notes.meaning: Jewish people received great blessings, especially because God gave them His written words in the Scriptures. Having God's law and promises gave them the true knowledge of God and His ways. This was a rich gift of grace, even though it came with great responsibility.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars take the phrase words of God to mean specifically God's promises of a coming Messiah or His covenant pledges to Israel, rather than the whole Old Testament.

notes.meaning: Paul answers another objection about the Jews who rejected God's message. Even if many people failed to believe and broke the covenant, human unbelief can never cancel God's promises. God remains completely faithful to what He has spoken.

Paul forcefully rejects the idea that God could ever break His word. Even if every human being proves false and untrustworthy, God will always be true to His character. Quoting King David's confession of sin, Paul shows that God is completely fair and right whenever He speaks and judges.

Someone might argue that if human wrongdoing makes God's fairness stand out more clearly, God would be unfair to punish it. Paul explains that he is only raising this argument to show how foolish human thinking can be. Even when human sin sets off God's goodness, sin remains fully guilty.

Paul completely dismisses the claim that God is unjust for punishing sin. If God could not punish sin that brings out His goodness, He would have no right to judge anyone at all. Everyone acknowledges that God is the true and fair Judge of all people.

Paul repeats the false argument from a personal viewpoint to show its flaw. An objector claims that if his own deceit makes God look even more truthful and glorious, he should not be condemned as a sinner. God's truth is displayed when He carries out His warnings, but that does not excuse the person who lied.

Some critics twisted Paul's message of free grace to claim that Christians encourage sin so that more good will follow. Paul flatly denies this false charge and warns that anyone who promotes such thinking deserves God's judgment. God never allows people to do wrong just because good might come from it.

Even though Jewish people had great religious privileges, they were in no better standing before God on their own merits than Gentiles. All people everywhere are trapped under the guilt and power of sin like slaves. No one can claim moral superiority before God's judgment.

Paul strings together Old Testament scriptures to prove that all people are trapped in sin. No one is naturally good, nobody truly understands spiritual truth on their own, and no one genuinely seeks after God. Everyone has wandered from God's path, becoming corrupt and useless like spoiled fruit.

Paul turns to the way sin corrupts human speech. He compares destructive talk to the foul air of an open grave and deadly snake venom hiding under the lips. Instead of blessing others, human mouths are naturally filled with angry cursing and bitter words.

Quoting the prophet Isaiah, Paul describes the violent and destructive actions of sinful people. They run quickly to harm others, leaving a trail of misery, heartbreak, and destruction behind them. Because they live selfishly, they have never known the path that leads to true peace.

This final quotation points out the root cause behind every sin. People act wickedly because they lack deep reverence and awe for God's holy presence and authority. Without respect for God, people feel free to pursue their own evil ways.

Paul reminds his readers that the Old Testament Scriptures were written first of all to the Jewish people who had the law. Since God's own people stand condemned by the law, all excuses and self-defense are silenced. The entire world stands guilty and held accountable before God's holy court.

To be justified means to be declared righteous and accepted by God. No human being can earn this standing by keeping the law, because everyone breaks it. The real purpose of the law is not to save people, but to show them what sin is and reveal their guilt.

differ.view: The works of the law refer primarily to the moral law, which remains in force and exposes sin, rather than merely ritual rules.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars argue that works of the law refers mainly to Jewish identity markers like circumcision and food laws, while other scholars maintain it includes all moral and legal obedience.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Works of the law specifically refers to the ceremonial and covenant requirements of the Mosaic Law, not to good works done through faith and grace.

notes.meaning: Paul turns to the good news that God has revealed His way of making sinners right with Himself without relying on human law-keeping. This rescue plan is not a surprise change, because the Old Testament Scriptures pointed to it and promised it long ago. Salvation comes through God's gracious gift rather than our own efforts.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The opening phrase But now marks a major turning point in history, signifying the arrival of the new era of the gospel in Christ rather than just a logical transition.

notes.meaning: God makes people right with Himself through faith in Jesus Christ, giving this gift to anyone who believes in Him. It makes no difference whether a person is a Jew or a Gentile. Everyone comes to God on the very same terms through trusting Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Several scholars translate the phrase as the faithfulness of Jesus Christ, seeing it as Christ's own obedient life and death on the cross rather than our faith directed toward Him.

notes.meaning: Every human being has broken God's commands and failed to live up to His holy standard. People have lost the reflection of God's perfect character and the honor for which they were created. Because everyone shares in this guilt, all people are in equal need of God's saving mercy.

differ.view: All people sinned in Adam as their covenant head, sharing both his guilt and an inherited sinful nature.

notes.meaning: God pardons sinners and accepts them as righteous entirely as a free gift, without any good works or merit of their own. Redemption means a ransom price was paid to buy back a slave. Jesus paid that full price through His death to free us from the penalty and power of sin.

God publicly displayed Jesus on the cross as the sacrifice that turns away His holy anger and covers our sins through faith in His shed blood. In past generations, God patiently held back the full punishment that sins deserved. Jesus' sacrifice showed that God never overlooked sin, providing a real payment for all who came before.

differ.view: Christ died as a propitiation to appease an offended God, upholding divine justice while making real forgiveness possible.
Christ's death was a propitiatory sacrifice that bore the wrath of God on behalf of believers to satisfy divine justice.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate the term as mercy seat, pointing directly to the cover of the ark where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement, while others translate it as an expiatory sacrifice that cleanses sin.

notes.meaning: By punishing sin at the cross, God proved His complete justice in the present age while freely forgiving those who trust in Jesus. God did not simply ignore His holy law, because the penalty for sin was truly paid in Christ. In this way, God is both perfectly fair and wonderfully merciful to believers.

Since salvation is entirely God's gift, no one has any room for pride or bragging about their heritage or good deeds. If being accepted by God depended on our own law-keeping, people could boast about their success. But because God saves us purely through faith in Christ, all human boasting is completely locked out.

Paul states the main conclusion of his teaching: a sinner is declared righteous before God solely through trusting in Christ, completely separate from any works of the law. Our own good deeds can never form the foundation for our acceptance with God. Salvation is received as an unearned gift by faith.

differ.view: Justification is received by faith alone without any human works, and this principle is the central message of the Christian faith.
Justification is by faith alone, meaning that no personal merit or good works ever form any part of the basis upon which God accepts a sinner.
Faith is the condition through which a person receives Christ, rather than a meritorious work in itself.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Justification is by faith but not by faith alone, since the word alone is not found in the original text, and true justification includes faith working through love rather than apart from it.

notes.meaning: Paul argues from the truth that there is only one true God. Because God made all people, He is not the God of Jewish people only, but of Gentiles as well. This one God justifies both circumcised Jews and uncircumcised Gentiles on the exact same terms through faith.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The question whether God is the God of Jews only indicates that works of the law refers to the Jewish ceremonial code of Moses.

notes.meaning: Teaching that we are saved by faith does not tear down or cancel God's law. Instead, faith upholds the law by honoring its holy demands, showing that Christ paid its full penalty, and empowering believers by the Holy Spirit to walk in obedience. Faith accomplishes what the law itself pointed toward all along.
